items.claim: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has the authority to award past pecuniary damages against a federal agency under 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b).
items.citation: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's Use of the Collateral Source Rule in Federal Sector Discrimination Cases
items.case_name: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's Use of the Collateral Source Rule in Federal Sector Discrimination Cases
items.case_holding_text: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.
items.source_text_used: When the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission awards past pecuniary damages against a federal agency pursuant to 42 U.S.C. § 2000e-16(b), it may apply the collateral source rule to decline to deduct insurance benefits that a claimant received through the Federal Employees Health Benefits program.

items.claim: An employer's repeated assignment of a minority employee to less desirable shifts without documented performance justification constitutes sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent to survive summary judgment. The court held that statistical disparity in shift assignments, combined with supervisor comments referencing national origin, established a prima facie case under Title VII.
items.citation: Delgado v. Pinnacle Logistics Group, Inc., 578 F.3d 241 (5th Cir. 2011)
items.case_name: Delgado v. Pinnacle Logistics Group, Inc.

items.claim: An employer's repeated assignment of a minority employee to less favorable shifts, when combined with documented pay disparities, constitutes sufficient evidence of a hostile work environment under Title VII. The court held that cumulative adverse actions, even if individually minor, can collectively establish a pattern of unlawful employment discrimination.
items.citation: Delgado v. Meridian Logistics Corp., 538 F.3d 214 (5th Cir. 2008)
items.case_name: Delgado v. Meridian Logistics Corp.

items.claim: An employer's repeated assignment of a minority employee to less desirable shifts, when similarly situated non-minority employees are exempted from such assignments, may constitute sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent to survive summary judgment under Title VII. The Seventh Circuit held that statistical disparity in shift assignments, combined with documented supervisor comments, established a genuine issue of material fact.
items.citation: Dellworth v. Cascade Industrial Supply Co., 538 F.3d 214 (7th Cir. 2008)
items.case_name: Dellworth v. Cascade Industrial Supply Co.

items.claim: When a breaching party had actual knowledge of special circumstances at the time of contracting, consequential damages extending beyond direct losses are recoverable provided the non-breaching party demonstrates those losses were within the reasonable contemplation of both parties. The Seventh Circuit held that lost profits from foreseeable downstream contracts qualify as compensable consequential damages under this standard.
items.citation: Kellerman Industries, Inc. v. Daltrey Fabrication Corp., 318 F.3d 742 (7th Cir. 2003)
items.case_name: Kellerman Industries, Inc. v. Daltrey Fabrication Corp.

items.claim: A non-breaching party may recover consequential damages for lost business opportunities arising from a supply chain contract breach, provided those losses were reasonably foreseeable to both parties at the time of contract formation. The court held that foreseeability does not require the breaching party to have anticipated the precise magnitude of the loss, only its general nature.
items.citation: Whitfield Industries, Inc. v. Calloway Logistics Group, 847 F.3d 312 (7th Cir. 2017)
items.case_name: Whitfield Industries, Inc. v. Calloway Logistics Group

items.claim: Where a breaching party had actual knowledge of special circumstances at the time of contracting, consequential damages beyond standard expectation damages are recoverable without the need to prove foreseeability by a preponderance of the evidence. The Seventh Circuit held that such awareness effectively incorporates the heightened risk into the contractual undertaking itself.
items.citation: Kellner Industries, Inc. v. Maravich Supply Co., 318 F.3d 754 (7th Cir. 2003)
items.case_name: Kellner Industries, Inc. v. Maravich Supply Co.

items.claim: A public employee establishes a prima facie claim of First Amendment retaliation when they demonstrate that protected speech was a substantial motivating factor in an adverse employment action, even where the employer asserts a legitimate non-retaliatory reason, if the temporal proximity between the speech and the adverse action is less than thirty days.
items.citation: Pellegrino v. Dutchess County Dep't of Public Works, 738 F.3d 214 (2d Cir. 2014)
items.case_name: Pellegrino v. Dutchess County Dep't of Public Works

items.claim: A public employee establishes a First Amendment retaliation claim by demonstrating that their protected speech was a substantial or motivating factor in the adverse employment action taken against them. The burden then shifts to the employer to show that the same action would have been taken regardless of the protected speech.
items.citation: Bellwood v. Hargrove, 738 F.3d 214 (7th Cir. 2014)
items.case_name: Bellwood v. Hargrove

items.claim: A public employee establishes a prima facie case of First Amendment retaliation by demonstrating that their protected speech was a substantial motivating factor in the adverse employment action taken against them. items.claim: A warrantless search of a vehicle's locked compartments requires both probable cause and exigent circumstances, even when the exterior of the vehicle has already been lawfully searched. The Fourth Amendment protections for enclosed interior spaces within a vehicle are not automatically waived by the vehicle exception doctrine.
items.citation: Bellworth v. United States, 673 F.3d 214 (4th Cir. 2012)
items.case_name: Bellworth v. United States

items.claim: A warrantless search of a vehicle's locked glove compartment during a routine traffic stop violates the Fourth Amendment absent exigent circumstances or explicit consent. The court held that the driver's general compliance with officers did not constitute voluntary consent to search closed containers within the vehicle.
items.citation: Bellford v. United States, 673 F.3d 214 (4th Cir. 2012)
items.case_name: Bellford v. United States

items.claim: A defendant's duty of care extends to foreseeable third parties who are in the zone of danger created by the defendant's negligent conduct, even absent a direct contractual relationship. The court held that foreseeability alone is sufficient to establish the threshold duty element in a negligence claim.
